annualCashFlows, whose row count is the fixed 25 year life.
sensitivityData, because the nine swept prices and the seven swept capex multipliers are what the table reports at each rank.
insights, which formats one of its five verdicts into each row.
explanation: One project goes in and each regime comes back with a complete life of its own, and every ledger inside annualCashFlows is 25 rows long whatever the regime.

prompt: All six templates on the default project return gross revenue of 2686.9277 million USD. What does that identical figure say about a fiscal regime?
options: The six templates happen to share a royalty base, and a template built on a different base would return a different revenue.
Cost recovery is struck before revenue is reported, so the revenue line is already net of the recoverable pool and equal by construction.
It touches neither production nor price, so revenue belongs to the field and only the division of it moves.
Revenue is the figure discounted at 10 percent, which removes the regime's effect on timing.
explanation: On that same 2686.9277 million USD, lifetime contractor net cash flow is 406.2057 million USD under Nigeria - PIA (2021) and 986.7327 under Generic Royalty/Tax.

prompt: The summary comes back sorted. What can be read off a row's position, and what tie break applies when two regimes match?
options: Contractor NPV descending, with the payback year as the secondary key wherever two NPVs are equal.
Contractor NPV descending and nothing else, and there is no secondary key at all, so equal NPVs keep the order they were passed in.
Contractor NPV descending and government cash flow ascending together, since the two mirror each other.
The internal rate of return descending, so rank 2 at 40.2125 percent above rank 3 at 44.0823 is an error.
explanation: summary[0] is the best regime for the contractor and nothing else can be read off a position, and the comparison exposes no option to sort on another column.

prompt: On the default project rank 2 returns an internal rate of return of 40.2125 percent and rank 3 returns 44.0823 percent. What has gone wrong?
options: The two rates were solved at different discount rates, because the bisection reruns each regime against its own hurdle.
The rank 2 regime failed to converge, so the solver reported the edge of its own bracket in that row instead of a root.
The rows were ordered on the payback year, which puts a regime with a later payout above one with a higher rate.
Nothing at all.
explanation: Generic Royalty/Tax leads on NPV at 397.0445 million USD with a rate of 44.6574 percent, and Brazil - Concession sits at rank 3 with 287.2804 and 44.0823, so the higher rate and the higher NPV belong to different regimes.

prompt: On ODIDI, Ghana - Deepwater sits at rank 3 collecting 308.8447 million USD for the government and USA - Gulf of Mexico at rank 4 collecting 277.6679. Why does the lower ranked regime collect less?
options: The take column is reported after royalty on that field, and USA - Gulf of Mexico charges the higher flat royalty of the two.
The sort key is NPV discounted at 12 percent while take is an undiscounted lifetime total, and the larger contractor sum arrives later.
The ranking was set by the government share of net revenue column, where 32.8219 percent sits below 36.5071 percent.
USA - Gulf of Mexico never pays back on ODIDI, so its take was truncated at the fixed 25 year horizon.
explanation: USA - Gulf of Mexico keeps 148.3166 million USD of lifetime contractor net cash flow against 117.1399 for Ghana - Deepwater and ranks lower anyway, paying back in year 7 against year 6.

prompt: Which regime is best for the government on ODIDI, and where is that read from?
options: The regime at rank 2, Generic Royalty/Tax, since the second row is the state's preference once the contractor's own pick is set aside.
Brazil - Concession at rank 1, because on a field where every NPV is negative the leading row is the one the state has squeezed hardest.
Angola - Deepwater PSC, read out of the take column at 316.7898 million USD, from rank 6.
Nigeria - PIA (2021), whose 36.9937 percent is the harshest rate of the six.
explanation: Nothing in the summary sorts by take, and quoting the second row as the government's preference is the exact claim the Insights tab used to make.

prompt: The summary's government share of net revenue column divides which two quantities?
options: Government cash flow over government cash flow plus contractor take, with total capex added back into the contractor's side.
Government cash flow over government cash flow plus contractor net cash flow, with no adjustment made to either quantity.
Total tax over total profit oil, which is why a template carrying no resource rent tax reads the lower number.
Government cash flow over gross revenue, which is why every template on one project shares a denominator.
explanation: Total capex on the default project is 500.0000 million USD and the same add-back goes into every row, which turns the denominator into revenue less opex, the net revenue the name refers to.

prompt: Angola - Deepwater PSC pays 245.1955 million USD of tax on the default project inside a take of 1263.7523, and its government share of net revenue reads 56.2797 percent. What is the column counting?
options: The corporate income tax of 25 percent and the resource rent tax of 50 percent, weighted by the years each of them was actually charged.
Tax over the contractor's profit share, which is the statutory rate this template was built to reproduce on a deepwater block.
The share of gross revenue the state received, which is why it exceeds 25 percent.
Royalty, the government's profit oil share and tax together, so most of what it counts is not tax.
explanation: USA - Gulf of Mexico is clearer still: its only tax is corporate income tax at 21 percent, its column reads 34.0485 percent, and a flat royalty contributes 503.7989 million USD of the 764.5528 collected.

prompt: On the published comparison built with capex of 20000, Brazil - Concession shows the gentlest government share of net revenue in the course, 13.5916 percent, on an NPV of -15354.6816 million USD. Why is it so low?
options: Brazil - Concession charges no royalty on that project, so only its corporate income tax and its resource rent tax reach the numerator.
The 20000 of capex was added back into the denominator and swamped everything else in it.
Cost recovery ran at the full limit for all 25 years, so the government's profit share never began and the tax base stayed at nought.
The rate is discounted at 10 percent while the take it divides is not.
explanation: A rate that falls as the project gets worse is not measuring the harshness of the terms. Angola - Deepwater PSC on the same comparison collects 1662.7835 million USD and reads 32.2800 percent.

prompt: What is the summary's government share of net revenue column not able to be compared with?
options: Another regime in the same table, because the capex added back differs by regime.
The same regime on a second field, because the add-back is discounted to that field's own valuation date before the ratio is struck.
A statutory rate, and government take on the price sweep, which reads 43.4694 percent where the column reads 33.7901.
The government cash flow column beside it, which the ratio is built from and therefore ranks in the same order on every project.
explanation: Both totals are undiscounted lifetime sums while the NPV beside them is discounted, and the same 500.0000 million USD add-back is applied to every row of one project.

prompt: paybackPeriod and rFactorPayoutYear sit next to each other in the summary. What is the difference between them?
options: Payback is the first year cumulative contractor cash after tax is above zero, and payout is the first year the R factor is above 1.0, a gross test that ignores the government.
Payback is discounted at the comparison's rate and payout is not, which is why payout arrives first.
Payback counts the year capex clears the cost pool, and payout the year the profit oil split first steps down a tranche.
They test the same event and differ only in rounding, payback down to the whole year and payout up.
explanation: USA - Gulf of Mexico on the default project runs cumulative contractor net cash flow of -310.0117, -140.2337 then 8.9905 million USD, and its R factor reads 0.512217, 0.922481 then 1.254640, so both land in year 3.

prompt: On the comparison built with capex of 20000 both year columns come back null for every regime. What does that null mean, and what does it not mean?
options: It means the bisection did not converge, so a longer horizon returns the same nulls.
It means the government collected nothing on that comparison, which is why the take column reads a flat 0.0000 beside it.
It means payback falls outside the swept price range and exists at an unswept price.
It means neither event happened inside the fixed 25 year horizon, and it is neither a zero nor a fast result.
explanation: The R factor never passes 1.0 there while the government still collects between 700.1194 and 1662.7835 million USD.

prompt: Both year columns are whole numbers with no interpolation. What does that cost a reader separating two regimes?
options: The columns round to the nearest year, so a regime turning positive halfway through year 4 reports year 4 or year 5 depending on the sign of that year's cash flow.
A project that turns positive in the first week of a year and one that turns positive in its last week report the same year.
Nothing at all, because both are computed on monthly cash flow inside the engine and only reported annually.
The years are discounted at 10 percent before they are rounded, which compresses a later year against an earlier one.
explanation: Neither column is discounted either, while the NPV standing beside them is, so the two year columns and the NPV are not measured on the same money.

prompt: The two Suite test regimes return Flat with an NPV of 1262.3470 million USD, take of 1881.7626 and a government share of net revenue of 36.5310, which is exactly the row Generic Royalty/Tax returns on the test project. Why?
options: Both rows were run at the same discount rate of 10 percent, and government share of net revenue is insensitive to everything except the rate.
The comparison caches one result per project and reuses it whenever the first regime in the list sorts to rank 1 of the summary.
The four instruments are identical, so a name is not a regime.
Generic Royalty/Tax is the fallback the engine substitutes for any regime that carries no resource rent tax and no tiered split.
explanation: One field and one deck divided by the same royalty, the same cost recovery, the same split and the same tax stack returns the same ledger under either label.

prompt: Which of these does the comparison refuse to do?
options: Accept a discount rate above 10 percent, which is why every published comparison in the course is run at that rate.
Accept more than six regimes in one call, which is the reason the template set was built with six members in it.
Vary the 25 year life, though it will accept a capex schedule spread across drilling, facilities and subsea in separate years.
Schedule capex, which it spends in year 1.
explanation: Every dollar of capex lands in year 1, the horizon is fixed at 25 years, and the model carries no abandonment, no depreciation, no loss carryforward and no ring fence.

prompt: How does the price sweep reach a swept oil price of 40 USD per bbl on the default project?
options: It overwrites the deck with a flat 40 USD per bbl, which removes the step at year 5 and the step at year 10.
It divides 40 by the first deck point's oil price of 70 and applies that multiplier to the oil price in every year of the deck.
It shifts every deck point down by the gap between 40 and 70, keeping the steps but not the ratios between them.
It rescales the base case NPV by the ratio of the two prices without re-running the ledger.
explanation: The multiplier moves the level and leaves the step structure intact, and every one of the nine points is a full re-run of the whole comparison.

prompt: There is no swept point between 70 and 80 USD per bbl. What is the line the chart draws across that gap?
options: A linear interpolation the engine returns beside the nine points, so any price inside the range can be quoted from it.
The engine's answer at the midpoint, because the sweep bisects each interval once to smooth the series it plots.
The chart's own line. The engine computed nine points and nothing between them.
A projection built from the climb, spread evenly across the range.
explanation: The nine prices are fixed at 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110 and 120 USD per bbl and no input changes them, so a project whose economics turn between two of them cannot be examined there.

prompt: At 40 USD per bbl the Designer's default production sharing regime leaves 5.9578 million USD of cost unrecovered at the end of the life. What does that say?
options: The cost recovery limit binds hard at the bottom of the sweep, and the pool closes to 0.7642 at 50 and to 0.0000 from 60 upward.
The pool carries forward past the horizon, so the contractor recovers the remainder in the following licence period.
The engine wrote the remainder off as an abandonment provision, which is what makes the NPV smaller than the loss.
Cost recovery was capped by the profit oil split rather than by the limit, since a low price walks the R factor into a generous tranche.
explanation: A limit that never binds at the deck price binds at 40 USD per bbl, where NPV is -51.1673 million USD and the engine names no internal rate of return at all.

The Nigeria - PIA (2021) template on the test project, the one project whose first deck point is not 70 USD per bbl.
The Designer's own default regime, id 1, Nigerian PIA (PSC).

prompt: For Generic Royalty/Tax the capex sweep reports a loss of 244.0782 million USD. Between which two points is that measured?

The NPV at a multiplier of 0.7 and the NPV at 1.3, which is the range the nine published capex cases are run over.

prompt: The capex verdict ranks one quantity per regime. Which quantity?

The fraction of base case NPV that survives a 50 percent overrun, which is why it reads as a percentage.

options: Quote the range rather than a figure, since a single template's reading is never a property of the field.
Quote the payout year of 6 instead, which reads the same under all six templates and so belongs to the field rather than to the terms.
Name the regime beside every reading, because both payback years and both totals are true of the same field.
Quote the highest of the six, since the best available terms bound what the field can be worth.
explanation: Payback in year 6 and payback in year 8 are both true of ODIDI, and a reading without its regime means nothing.

prompt: The capstone method proves two rows by hand and reads the remaining twenty three. What is it blind to?
options: A tier crossing, a deck step and a pool that refills late in life, none of which appear in the two rows it proves.
A royalty taken on the wrong base, since an error of that kind only shows itself once the cumulative column has been totalled.
A tax charged where profit oil is 0.0000, which the year 1 row cannot reveal.
A capex spread across the early years instead of landing whole in year 1, since the year 4 row would still balance under either treatment.
explanation: Nothing in the method discounts anything either, so ODIDI's value of -37.3123 under those terms is invisible to it.

prompt: ODIDI under Brazil returns 192.9896 of contractor cash over 25 years and a value of -5.8662 at 12 percent. Which reading is wrong?
options: The value, because a life that returns positive cash cannot be worth less than nothing.
Neither. Both are readings of the same 25 rows, and the Associate answer quotes each with its basis.
The total, because it adds year 25 money to year 1 money and so overstates what came back.
The pair, because a total and a value that disagree in sign cannot both be readings of one ledger.
explanation: Which of the two a decision rests on takes a discount convention, and every one of the six templates on ODIDI shows the same pair of signs.

prompt: What can the Associate reading of ODIDI, which puts the state's collection between 232.9950 and 316.7898, not say?
options: Which template collects the most, since two collections are only comparable when the closing unrecovered pools of the two ledgers are equal.
Which template leaves the contractor the most cash over the life of the field, which is a ranking that needs a discount convention this tier does not carry.
How much of each collection came from royalty rather than from tax.
Which of those splits is fair, which survives a price collapse, and which numbers on a comparison screen are measurements at all.
explanation: The contractor keeps between 109.1947 and 192.9896 across the same six templates, and stating the range is not judging it.

prompt: Every template in the Associate tier was read at one setting, yet three of the six carry an instrument that moves on its own. Which are they?
options: A cost recovery limit that tightens automatically as the standing pool grows, and a minimum tax that arms itself once the residual has fallen far enough.
A corporate rate that steps with the R factor, and a royalty that steps with cumulative production.
A royalty keyed on the oil price and a profit split keyed on the R factor, which under PIA steps the share from 60 to 40 to 30 percent.
A discount rate that follows the price deck from one year to the next, and a profit split that follows the closing unrecovered pool of the year before it.
explanation: The R factor is a ratio of cumulatives, so it can fall back below a threshold it passed and step the contractor's share up again.

prompt: What is a fiscal regime, as this engine represents one?
options: Whatever the jurisdiction's fiscal code contains, since each template is a reading of the statute it is named for and the engine executes that reading.
The four fields together with a signature bonus and a state participation share, which the templates carry as separate entries beside the tax block.
Four fields on one object: a royalty, a cost recovery limit, a profit split, and a tax block holding cit, rrt, minTax and an optional rrtUpliftPct.
A royalty and a tax, with the cost recovery limit and the profit split supplied by the project inputs rather than by the regime.
explanation: Nothing else exists. A regime that needs an instrument outside those four cannot be expressed in this sandbox at all.

prompt: A regime sets cit and rrt and omits rrtUpliftPct entirely. What uplift does the run charge?
options: 20 percent, the documented default the engine substitutes whenever the field is absent.
Zero, because a field that was never supplied cannot grant relief, so the resource rent tax falls on the profit share itself.
The same figure as rrt, since the uplift is written as a fraction of the resource rent tax rate it belongs to.
None, and the run refuses the regime until an uplift is supplied for it.
explanation: The uplift is optional in the object and defaults to 20, so a template that says nothing about it is not running without one.

prompt: Nigeria - PIA (2021) and Generic Royalty/Tax both carry CIT 30 percent, RRT 0 percent and minimum tax 0 percent, yet on the Designer's default project the contractor keeps 406.2057 million USD under one and 986.7327 million USD under the other. What opened that gap?
options: A heavier tax bill under the PIA terms, which totals 422.8854 million USD over the life against 174.0882 million USD for the Generic terms.
The other three fields, a cost recovery limit of 80 percent instead of 100 and an R factor split of 60, then 40, then 30 percent instead of a flat 100 percent to the contractor.
A larger royalty under the PIA slider, which collects 335.8660 million USD against the 268.6928 million USD the Generic rate collects.
Different sales, since the PIA line is run against a lower price deck than the Generic line is.
explanation: The PIA line pays the smaller tax of the two, 174.0882 million USD against 422.8854, and the smaller royalty, 268.6928 against 335.8660. A tax rate quoted on its own predicts nothing.

prompt: Six templates are run on the published test project. What does the total revenue column read down those six lines?
options: It falls as the royalty rate rises, since royalty is charged on the top line before anything else is deducted from it.
It moves by a few million USD, because each template recovers cost at a different limit and cost recovery is netted against sales.
It reads 2686.9277 million USD, which is the revenue figure every comparison in this sandbox reports.
7001.1938 million USD on every one of them, because a regime touches neither production nor price.
explanation: 2686.9277 million USD is the default project's constant. Whichever project is loaded, the revenue column is the same on all six lines, so any spread in the answer is the regime.

prompt: Which project input shortens the sandbox horizon below 25 years?
options: None of them. PROJECT_LIFE is 25 rows and the engine returns 25 rows for every regime and every project.
The economic limit, reached in the year opex first exceeds gross revenue, after which the remaining rows are dropped from the totals.
The price deck, whose last dated point closes the profile in the year that point falls in.
A steep decline, which ends the profile once the rate has fallen far enough below the initial rate.
explanation: There is no input anywhere that changes 25 to another number, which is why year 25 of the default project still produces 0.291148 million bbl.

prompt: The published case that puts capex of 20000 on the test project reports payback year null and payout year null. What does that say about its 25 rows?
options: The engine truncated the run in the year the pool was judged unrecoverable, so the totals cover fewer than 25 rows.
The rows after the loss were computed but left out of government cash flow, which is why that figure stops at 875.1492 million USD.
Nothing stopped. All 25 were computed, taxed and counted into the totals, and null records only that cumulative contractor net cash flow never rose above zero.
The project was abandoned inside the model, and the abandonment charge is the closing pool of 15724.0151 million USD.
explanation: Reading null as a stop is how a reader ends up quoting a 25 year royalty stream as a short one. Total contractor net cash flow on that case is -15724.0151 million USD.

prompt: On that same 20000 capex case the treasury collects 875.1492 million USD. Which instrument delivered it?
options: The minimum tax, which floors the government at a percent of gross revenue in any year the profit share collapses.
Royalty alone, since total profit oil and total tax are both 0.0000 million USD there.
Cost recovery, which hands the unrecovered pool back to the state once the horizon ends without clearing it.
Resource rent tax charged on the negative cash flow, against the capital uplift the tax block carries.
explanation: No abandonment and no economic limit exist to stop the field, so it produces for 25 years and pays royalty on total revenue of 7001.1938 million USD while losing money.

prompt: A template field reads 18.75 and the derived rate column beside the royalty reads 0.187500. How do the two relate?
options: The column is the rate after the cost recovery limit has been applied to it, which is why it prints so much smaller than the field does.
The field is quoted on gross revenue and the column on revenue after royalty, so the two differ by the royalty itself.
The column is a rate of 0.187500 percent, which is what a royalty of 50.9979 million USD on 271.9889 million USD of revenue works out at.
They are one instrument in two conventions, a percent and a ratio.
explanation: A rate of 0.187500 percent charged on gross revenue of 271.9889 million USD could never produce the 50.9979 million USD the royalty column prints.

prompt: Year 1 gross revenue on the Designer's default project prints as 271.9889. In what unit?
options: United States dollars, which makes the year 1 capex charge of 500.0000 a rounding error.
Millions of United States dollars, so 271.9889 million USD against a capex row of 500.0000 million USD.
Millions of barrels of oil equivalent, converted at 6000 scf per barrel before the deck price for the year is applied.
Millions of United States dollars on a real basis, restated to year 1 money by the deflator the sandbox carries.
explanation: Money is millions of USD everywhere in the ledger, printed to four decimals and quoted as printed. A reader who carries 271.9889 as USD believes the project pays back instantly.

prompt: What is the 6000 scf per barrel conversion used for in this model?
options: The variable half of opex, which is charged in USD per boe, and nothing else.
Gross revenue, where the three streams are priced as one boe total.
The royalty base, charging gas and NGL at the oil rate.
The R factor, whose cumulative revenue is expressed in boe before it is divided by cumulative cost.
explanation: Revenue prices each stream at its own deck point. The engine writes the boe conversion as a multiply by 1000 and a divide by 6000, and the variable opex rate is the only place it is needed.

prompt: Year 1 of the default project shows oil at 3.650000 and gas at 0.018250. Is the gas negligible?
options: Yes, and the published case that adds gas and NGL to the default project confirms it by leaving total revenue unchanged.
Yes, since a stream contributing under one percent of the volume is dropped from the boe total the variable opex is charged on.
The comparison cannot be made from those two figures, because oil is in million bbl and gas is in million Mscf.
No, because the gas column has already been converted to barrels of oil equivalent at 6000 scf per barrel.
explanation: The two columns are not on the same axis at all. The oil and NGL columns are million bbl and the gas column is million Mscf.

prompt: Why is subtracting the two printed endpoints of a derived column and matching the printed difference a bad check?
options: The printed endpoints belong to different rows of the ledger, while a derived difference is only ever computed within one row.
A derived column is computed at full precision and then rounded, and its endpoints are rounded too, so a printed pair of 79.2711 and 79.4678 carries a printed climb of 0.1968.
A derived column is an estimate the engine never returns, so it carries no defined precision to check anything against.
Derived columns print to six decimals and returned columns to four, so the two can never be put in the same subtraction.
explanation: Both figures are correct and the hand subtraction is off by one in the last place. The default project's Generic Royalty/Tax pair does the same thing, printing 51.2558 and 41.0660 against a climb of -10.1897.

prompt: What separates a million USD in year 25 from a million USD in year 1 here?
options: An escalation carried by the price deck past its last dated point.
A real basis, so every row prints in year 1 money.
A valuation date the rows are restated against.
Only the discount exponent, since there is no inflation and no deflator anywhere.
explanation: The units refuse to carry a currency year. A row is a year and the year is its own discount exponent, and nothing else distinguishes the two.

prompt: The engine header names a single source of truth for Nigerian fiscal math. What is this model for?
options: Comparing the shape of regimes against each other, with the Petroleum Economics Studio engine holding the fiscal truth.
Assessing a Nigerian liability under the Petroleum Industry Act, which is why the template set carries a PIA entry at all.
Producing a filing figure, once a template has been reconciled against the Petroleum Economics Studio engine on the same project.
Replacing that engine for screening work, since the two agree on a total government cash flow of 1339.2784 million USD.
explanation: A template named for a jurisdiction is a caricature in six numbers, useful for asking which instrument moved which result and unfit for filing anything.

prompt: A term sheet carries a signature bonus, a domestic supply obligation and a state participation share. How are the three entered?
options: The bonus goes into a capex bucket, the obligation into the variable opex rate, and the participation share into the contractor split.
Each becomes a tier on the profit split, the one field taking more than one entry.
They are not. A regime needing any of them cannot be expressed in this sandbox at all.
They ride on the template's description string into government cash flow.
explanation: There is no signature bonus, no domestic supply obligation, no state participation and no flare penalty. Four fields, and the ledger they act on, are the whole of it.

prompt: The Designer's default project declares oil at 10000 bbl/d declining 10 percent a year, and year 1 comes back as 3.650000 million bbl. Why is there no decline in that first figure?
options: A mid year convention takes half a year of decline in year 1, and at a 10 percent decline the half year rounds away before the figure is printed.
Year 1 is a stub the engine leaves flat, and the exponential starts from the first full year of production after it.
The decline is applied after the year is booked, so year 1 is the initial rate times 365 days and the first reduction lands in year 2.
The declared decline is nominal rather than effective, so nothing is lost in year 1 and the later years lose more.
explanation: The check is arithmetic you can do in your head: year 1 in million bbl is the daily rate times 365 divided by one million, exactly. ODIDI at 8000 bbl/d gives 2.920000 the same way.

prompt: generateProductionProfile is not exported. How are the annual volumes recovered from the engine?
options: By reading them out of the returned object, which records each stream beside the revenue that stream produced in the year.
By dividing the printed gross revenue by the applied oil price, which the engine reports in a column of its own.
By rebuilding them from the declared rate and decline, since no exported quantity depends on volume alone.
By a probe: royalty zero, a 100 percent limit, a flat 100 percent split, every tax at zero, two streams zeroed and the survivor priced at 1.0.
explanation: grossRevenue then returns that stream's annual volume divided by one million, which is why the oil and NGL columns read million bbl and the gas column million Mscf.

prompt: Year 25 of the default project still produces 0.291148 million bbl of oil and still pays 11.5851 million USD of opex. What ends the field?
options: The fixed horizon of 25 rows and nothing else, because the sandbox carries no economic limit.
The year opex overtakes gross revenue, which on this project is year 25 at 11.5851 against 24.3216 million USD.
The last dated point on the price deck, since no revenue can be computed for a year the deck does not reach.
Exhaustion of the profile, an exponential decline having taken the rate to zero by the end of the horizon.
explanation: Year 25 pays 11.5851 million USD of opex against 24.3216 million USD of revenue, so it happens to pay. Nothing would have stopped it if it did not.

prompt: Between year 1 and year 25 the default gas column falls from 0.018250 to 0.002467 while the NGL column falls from 0.547500 to 0.025466. What does that show?
options: Gas is held up late in life by the deck, whose gas points keep stepping while the liquid points have run out.
Each stream declines at its own rate, and the 8 percent gas stream keeps a larger fraction of itself than the 12 percent NGL stream.
The engine floors a stream once it falls far enough below its initial rate, which is what flattens the gas tail.
NGL is produced as a yield off the gas stream, so it has to fall faster than the gas it comes from.
explanation: Three independent exponentials. ODIDI shows the same thing harder, gas at 9 percent going from 0.014600 to 0.001518 while NGL at 15 percent goes from 0.328500 to 0.006646.

prompt: The published test project declares gas at 0 Mscf/d and NGL at 0 bbl/d, each with a decline of 0 percent. What does the engine do with the two streams?
options: It drops both and returns a single stream project, which is how the test project reaches total revenue of 7001.1938 million USD on one declining oil stream.
It generates a column of zeros for all 25 years, contributing 0.0000 to revenue and no boe to opex, which is not the same as skipping them.
It reads a decline of 0 percent as a flat stream held at its initial rate, so both columns are constant instead of declining.
It refuses the project, since a stream must carry a positive initial rate before any decline can be applied to it.
explanation: A zero stream is present and priced. The test project is a useful control precisely because those two columns are zeros rather than absences.

prompt: What relationship does the sandbox model between the oil, gas and NGL streams?
options: A gas oil ratio, which ties the gas rate to the oil rate declared for the project and declines along with it.
A condensate yield, so the NGL volume is computed off the gas volume rather than from an initial rate of its own.
A shrinkage and fuel deduction, taken off the gas stream before it reaches the revenue sum or the boe sum.
None. Three independent exponentials, summed once in revenue and again in boe.
explanation: There is no gas oil ratio, no yield, no shrinkage and no flare deduction. Each stream carries only an initial rate and a decline.

prompt: The default deck prices oil at 70 in year 1 and 75 in year 5. What price is applied in years 2, 3 and 4?
options: 70.000000 USD per bbl in each of them, because getPriceForYear holds the last point reached and never interpolates.
A straight line drawn between the two dated points, so that the three years climb steadily from 70.000000 towards 75.000000 USD per bbl.
75.000000 USD per bbl, since the next dated point is known and the engine prices forward to it.
The average of the two dated points, held flat until the year 5 point takes over from it.
explanation: The whole move from 70.000000 to 75.000000 arrives in a single row. A deck is a staircase, and nothing between two points is interpolated.

prompt: The default deck's last dated point is year 10 at 80 USD per bbl. What is applied in year 25?
options: A price grown from 80.000000 at the project discount rate of 10 percent a year, which is the escalation this model applies.
Nothing, the deck having run out and the revenue column ending with its last dated point.
80.000000 USD per bbl, unchanged, because the engine does not escalate past the last point on a deck.
The year 10 price adjusted for the fall in volume, so that the revenue column declines smoothly to the end.
explanation: Sixteen consecutive years sit at 80.000000 USD per bbl. A reader expecting annual escalation carries a growing shortfall from year 10 to year 25 and cannot find it, because no output column reports a price.

prompt: ODIDI steps from 45 to 65 USD per bbl at year 6 and its revenue rises from 76.1939 to 93.9859 million USD. The default project steps from 70 to 75 at year 5 and its revenue falls from 197.5024 to 191.1513. Why the opposite signs?
options: The default step lands in a year where the deck also lowers its gas and NGL points, which cancels the gain on oil.
The size of the step against the size of the decline. A 5 USD step does not outrun a 10 percent oil decline, and a 20 USD step does outrun a 14 percent one.
ODIDI's step is the second point on its deck and the default step is the third, and only a second point is applied in full.
Volume rose in ODIDI at year 6, a price step lifting the rate the profile is generated from.
explanation: Every ODIDI stream fell in year 6. The whole of the rise from 76.1939 to 93.9859 million USD is the deck.

prompt: Which column of the returned ledger reports the price the engine used for a year?
options: The deck column, which the engine copies out of the project inputs into every row of the ledger it returns.
The implied rate column, which carries the price the royalty tier for that year was selected on.
The rFactor column, whose numerator is cumulative revenue and therefore the prices behind each year of it.
None of them. The applied price is recovered by dividing revenue by volume in a single stream probe.
explanation: Nothing in the output says which deck was used, which is why a deck read wrongly produces a shortfall with no column to trace it to.

prompt: Default project opex reads 31.0027 million USD in year 1 and 11.5851 in year 25, against a fixed figure of 10 million USD a year. What is moving?
options: The variable half, 5 USD per boe on a declining boe total, which is why the curve heads towards the fixed number.
The fixed half, which the engine escalates through the early years and relaxes as the field matures.
The regime, since opex enters the cost pool and the pool is drawn down over the life of the field.
The deck, because the variable rate is charged against revenue rather than against the barrels produced, and revenue steps at year 5.
explanation: Almost the whole of the year 25 bill of 11.5851 million USD is the fixed 10 million USD a year. The curve would only reach it if production reached zero, which the horizon ends first.

prompt: ODIDI runs a variable rate of 4 USD per boe against the default project's 5, yet its year 25 opex of 12.3405 million USD is above the default project's 11.5851. How?
options: ODIDI produces more boe in year 25, its gas decline of 9 percent being slower than the default project's 8 percent.
ODIDI's discount rate of 12 percent is applied to the cost columns, which lifts every year in the tail.
By year 25 almost the whole bill is fixed, and ODIDI's fixed figure is 12 million USD a year against 10.
The variable rate is charged on revenue, and ODIDI's deck prices oil at 85 USD per bbl in year 25 against 80.
explanation: ODIDI starts well below the default project, at 25.0037 million USD against 31.0027, and ends above it. The fixed half decides the tail.

prompt: The default deck steps oil from 70 to 75 USD per bbl at year 5, and opex moves from 25.1816 to 23.6264 million USD. Why did the cost fall in a year the price rose?
options: The variable rate is charged on revenue after royalty, which fell that year even though the oil price rose.
Opex tracks boe, and boe does not know what a barrel sold for.
The fixed half is prorated against the deck, so a higher price lowers the fixed charge carried in the year.
The step is applied at the end of the year, so year 5 costs are still computed at 70.000000 USD per bbl.
explanation: Opex is fixed plus the variable rate times the boe produced, divided by one million. Price enters revenue and nothing else.

prompt: A development is to be built over three years. How is the schedule entered?
options: It is not. Capex is one sum charged to year 1, 500.0000 million USD on the default project and 420.0000 on ODIDI, and the multiplier scales the total rather than the timing.
By splitting the three buckets, since drilling, facilities and subsea are each charged in the year the engine assigns them.
By setting the capex multiplier below one and running the remainder as a second project, which spreads the same total.
By lowering the multiplier to 0.7, which moves the spend later and lifts NPV to 1460.6941 million USD on the flat regime.
explanation: The sandbox refuses a capex schedule and has no field to hold one. Faking it with the multiplier changes the total and quietly answers a different question.

prompt: Six regimes are compared on one project. What do their opex and capex columns look like?
options: They part at the cost recovery limit, which caps how much of each year's cost the ledger admits in the first place.
They part once the pool clears, since unrecovered cost is written back out of the opex column in the year that happens.
They part in year 1 only, where the capex charge is netted against the royalty the regime takes off the top line.
Identical, row for row, because nothing a government does in this model changes what the field costs.
explanation: The cost columns do not depend on the regime. Over the life the default project spends 441.4436 million USD of opex and ODIDI spends 390.2137 million USD, whichever template is loaded.

prompt: How is the gross revenue row built?
options: The three streams converted to boe at 6000 scf per barrel and then priced at the deck's oil point for the year.
Volumes at deck prices less the transport and processing the project declares, which is what states the row in millions of USD.
Oil volume times the applied oil price, plus gas times its price, plus NGL times its price, all divided by one million.
Oil at the deck price plus the gas and NGL taken at a fraction of it, the deck carrying only one dated series.
explanation: The divide by one million is what puts the ledger in millions of USD. Year 1 of the default project is 271.9889 million USD and year 25 is 24.3216.

prompt: What is the royalty charged on?
options: Gross revenue, before any cost is deducted and before anything else in the ledger happens.
Revenue after opex, which is the netback a production sharing contract normally charges a royalty against.
Revenue after cost recovery, so that the cost pool is served before the state takes a share of the year.
Profit oil, royalty and the profit split being the two instruments that divide what is left once cost is met.
explanation: Year 1 of the default project pays 50.9979 million USD of royalty on 271.9889 million USD of revenue. Nothing has been deducted from the base.

prompt: The implied rate column under USA - Gulf of Mexico reads 0.187500 in year 1, in year 5 and in year 25 of the default project. What has that demonstrated?
options: That the deck holds one oil price across those years, since the implied rate would move with the price if it did not.
That the royalty really is flat, proved from the two printed columns rather than assumed from the template field of 18.75.
That the royalty is charged on a base declining at the same rate as revenue, which is what holds the ratio still.
That the rate has been checked in the three years where a check is possible, the deck steps being the years where it is not.
explanation: Royalty is 50.9979 million USD on 271.9889 in year 1 and 4.5603 on 24.3216 in year 25. One rate, one base, twenty five years.

prompt: Year 1 of the default project under the Gulf of Mexico terms carries capex of 500.0000 million USD and a contractor net cash flow of -310.0117. What royalty is charged that year?
options: Nothing, since a royalty is charged on revenue after royalty and no profit oil arises in the year the capex lands.
A reduced charge, the sandbox waiving royalty in a year that closes below zero.
50.9979 million USD, which then enters the unrecovered cost pool and comes back to the contractor in a later year.
50.9979 million USD, the full rate on the top line, and that is the whole of government cash flow for the year.
explanation: A loss making year pays royalty at the same rate as the best year in the field. There is no profit oil and no tax in year 1, so government cash flow is the royalty alone.

prompt: Which column of the returned ledger holds revenue after royalty?
options: The costRecovered column, which equals it whenever the limit is 100 percent and the pool is deep enough to absorb the whole of the year's cost.
The profitOil column, which is revenue after royalty once the profit split has been applied to it.
No column does. It is the difference of two printed columns, and it is the base the cost recovery limit is a percent of.
The grossRevenue column, the royalty being settled outside the ledger and never entering the revenue row that the recovery limit is taken on.
explanation: Under the Gulf of Mexico terms year 1 of the default project carries revenue after royalty of 220.9910 million USD, and that is the ceiling a 100 percent limit gives.

prompt: In year 1 of the default project revenue after royalty is 220.9910 million USD and the costs are capex of 500.0000 and opex of 31.0027. What does a cost recovery limit of 100 percent do?
options: Nothing, a 100 percent limit not being a limit, so the whole of the year's cost is recovered against it.
It binds. The ceiling of 220.9910 million USD is below the capex charge on its own, so costRecovered stops there and the pool closes at 310.0117 million USD.
It caps recovery at 271.9889 million USD, the year's gross revenue being what a 100 percent limit is a percent of.
It leaves the capex in the pool untouched and recovers the opex of 31.0027 million USD, the recoverable half in a capex year.
explanation: A 100 percent limit is not the same thing as recovering everything. It binds whenever the year's costs exceed its revenue after royalty, which a year one capex charge guarantees.

prompt: A reader takes the cost recovery ceiling as a percent of gross revenue instead. How large is the error in year 1 of the default project?
options: Exactly the royalty, 50.9979 million USD of extra recovery, which then flows into the pool, into the R factor and into every split keyed on it.
It is immaterial at a 100 percent limit, since the ceiling binds either way in the year the capex lands.
It is the spread between the two limits the template set uses, 80 percent against 100, applied to the year's revenue.
It cancels in the totals, a larger recovery in year 1 leaving a smaller pool for the years that follow it.
explanation: The tell is worth memorising: if a cost recovery ceiling ever equals gross revenue, the wrong base has been used, because royalty is always taken first.

prompt: Angola - Deepwater PSC charges a royalty of 0 percent and collects 0.0000 million USD on the default project, yet its contractor keeps 481.7318 million USD against 980.9313 under the Gulf of Mexico terms. Why?
options: Its production is lower, the Angola template being run on a deepwater profile rather than on the Designer's default project.
Its royalty is collected later as an additional entitlement, which the template description records and the run applies at the end.
Its CIT of 25 percent is charged on gross revenue rather than on the contractor profit share, which is the harsher base.
Its other three fields are hard: cost recovery capped at 50 percent, a tiered profit split, and RRT at 50 percent.
explanation: A low headline rate is not a soft regime. The template with no royalty at all is the harsher of the two here.

prompt: Nigeria - PIA (2021) collects total royalty of 268.6928 million USD on the default project and 700.1194 on the test project, and Brazil - Concession collects exactly the same on both. How does a slider match a flat 10 percent?
options: The engine averages a sliding scale over the life of the field and charges one mean rate, which for tiers of 7.5 and 10 percent works out at 10 percent on both decks.
The slider keys on the first dated point of the deck, which is above 50 USD per bbl on both projects, and that point then fixes the rate for the whole of the 25 year run.
Every applied price on both decks is above the 50 USD per bbl threshold, so the slider sits in its 10 percent tier in every year and never slides.
A sliding royalty falls back to the flat rate of the nearest template whenever its two tiers straddle the deck.
explanation: The default deck prices oil at 70, 75 and 80 USD per bbl and the test deck at 80. A sliding instrument that never slides is a flat one, and whether it slides is a property of the deck.
