prompt: The teaching field summary is sorted by contractor net present value descending and Brazil - Concession is first at negative 5.8662 million USD. Government cash flow runs the other way, 316.7898 for Angola against 232.9950 for Brazil. Which order is right?
options: The take order, since a present value that is negative for every regime cannot rank anything and should not be sorted on at all.
The present value order, because the summary's own sort is the engine's verdict and the take column is a derived quantity beside it.
Neither, because the two disagree, and a ranking that reverses under a second column is evidence that the comparison was mis-specified.
Both, and they are orders of different things.
explanation: The best regime for the contractor on that field has a present value of negative 5.8662 million USD. Being least bad is a real answer, and it needs its label saying so.

prompt: Three of the six templates split profit oil on the R factor. What does a year in which the contractor's tranche is 0.300000 do to the tax base?
options: It leaves the whole of profit oil taxable, since the tax is charged before the split and the split then divides what is left of it.
It leaves 0.300000 of profit oil taxable and charges the government's share at the same rate, which the take column reports on its own.
It leaves only the contractor's 0.300000 of profit oil taxable, because the government's share of profit oil never passes through the tax line.
It leaves the whole of profit oil taxable but at 0.300000 of the rate, which is how a split is expressed inside the stack.
explanation: In year 11 of the default project a tranche of 0.300000 on 80.0217 million USD of profit oil leaves a base of 24.0065, which is how Ghana - Deepwater collects 230.9340 over the life at 35 percent while Generic Royalty/Tax collects 422.8854 at 30.

prompt: In year 3 of the published crossing case profit oil jumps from 46.2528 to 179.0750 million USD while the contractor's split falls from 0.600000 to 0.400000. Is the contractor worse off?
options: No. A larger share of a much smaller quantity is less money than a smaller share of a much larger one, and the pool clearing is what released the profit oil.
Yes, because the tranche crossing takes a fifth of the contractor's profit oil away in the year it happens.
Yes, because a split falling in the same year that profit oil rises means the government captured the whole of the increase.
It cannot be told from those figures, because the split applies to cost oil as well and that column is not shown.
explanation: A split rate and a share of money are different quantities and can move in opposite directions in one row. Cost recovery cleared and the tranche crossed in the same year.

prompt: Two runs of the same regime on the same project differ only in the resource rent tax uplift, one taking the default and one set to 0. Total tax is 2127.5549 million USD against 2207.5549 and present value at 10 percent 831.8148 against 777.1737. What moved them?
options: The discount rate, since the two runs are reported at different rates and only one of them is the project's own.
One field left out of the inputs, which took its documented default of 20 percent and opened the larger of the two relief pools.
The cost recovery limit, which is the only input that can move a present value and a total tax together on one project.
A minimum tax that bound in one run and not the other, which changed the years the charge falls in and therefore the discounting.
explanation: The two ledgers differ in one year only, year 4, at 169.6803 against 249.6803 million USD. A default worth 80 million USD of tax is worth reading in the inputs and not in the output.

prompt: One published run reaches payback only in year 12, closes at negative 111.7254 million USD of present value and is given no rate of return at all, and it still hands over 177.3774 of royalty. What do those readings show together?
options: That the royalty is the reason the rate of return is so low, since an instrument charged before cost is what a marginal project cannot carry.
That the present value is the binding reading, because a charge on revenue is waived in any year a project earns less than its discount rate.
That the two readings belong to different runs, since a project that pays back at all cannot also carry a negative present value.
A royalty is charged on gross revenue whether or not the project makes money.
explanation: The royalty collected is more than twice the contractor's whole lifetime cash flow of 80.8085 million USD. The instrument sees a price, picks a rate and charges gross revenue.

prompt: A test project run at 20000 of capex closes with 15724.0151 million USD in the pool and reports a contractor net cash flow of negative 15724.0151. What does its rate of return column say?
options: Null, with the status no-sign-change, since a ledger carrying no positive contractor cash flow in any year never changes sign.
0.0000 percent, from the check on the present value at a rate of zero, which is not above zero on this ledger.
Null, with the status no-root, because no rate from negative 99 to 1000 percent brings its present value to zero.
A negative rate, since a project that never recovers its outlay solves to a root below zero.
explanation: Present value at 10 percent is negative 15453.8510 million USD, government cash flow is 875.1492 and all of it is royalty, because royalty does not wait for cost to be recovered.

prompt: On the teaching field under the PIA template the implied royalty rate steps from 0.075000 to 0.100000 in year 6, and the R factor crosses 1.0 in the same year, from 0.997329 to 1.136133. Are those the same event?
options: Yes. Reaching payout is what moves a field into the upper royalty tier, which is why both columns change in the same row.
No. The royalty moved because the deck steps to 65 USD per bbl in year 6, and the ratio crossed because cumulative revenue overtook cumulative cost.
Yes, because both instruments read the applied oil price, and a deck step therefore moves the royalty tier and the ratio together.
No, and the royalty step is the earlier of the two, since a price event reaches the ledger a year before a cumulative one can.
explanation: One is a price event and the other is a cumulative one, and this field is the only teaching case where a royalty tier changes inside the life.

prompt: Every regime on the teaching field reports an R factor payout year of 6, while payback years run 6 for Brazil - Concession, 7 for Generic Royalty/Tax and 8 for Angola - Deepwater PSC. Why does one agree across regimes and the other not?
options: Payout is the first year the R factor is above 1.0 and the ratio is net of nothing fiscal, while payback is the first year cumulative contractor net cash flow turns positive and that is net of royalty, tax and the split.
Payout is computed from the summary and payback from the ledger, and the two are produced by different functions on different projects.
Payout is rounded to the nearest year across the six regimes, while payback is reported exactly as each ledger returns it.
Payback moves because each regime carries a different cost recovery limit, and payout does not because the limit is applied after the ratio.
explanation: The R factor responds only to production, price and cost. Two measures that agree on one project encourage the habit of treating them as one, and they are not.

prompt: What does this sandbox refuse to be?
options: A comparison of the shapes of regimes, which requires the real fiscal codes rather than four instruments on one ledger.
A model of the timing of cost recovery, since the pool it carries has no schedule and cannot represent a real recovery profile.
A ledger for a field with more than one product stream, because only the oil price selects a royalty tier.
A second fiscal truth, and a source of any number quotable as a tax liability.
explanation: The module's single source of truth for Nigerian fiscal math is the Petroleum Economics Studio engine. A comparison of shapes is worth a great deal; a number lifted out of it and quoted as a liability is worth nothing.

prompt: Three probe decks on the Designer's default project, priced at 49.990000, 50.000000 and 50.010000 USD per bbl, are run against the PIA royalty tiers of 0 USD/bbl at 7.5 percent and 50 USD/bbl at 10 percent. What rate does the deck priced exactly at the threshold pay?
options: 0.075000, the lower tier, because a threshold is the price at which the next tier BEGINS and a price merely equal to it has not yet passed into the band above.
The mean of the two tiers, because the engine interpolates the rate over the last cent of approach to a threshold rather than jumping.
0.100000, the upper tier, on gross revenue of 198.9889 giving a royalty of 19.8989.
0.075000, because the walk stops at the first tier whose threshold is not yet strictly exceeded and keeps the rate it was holding.
explanation: The comparison in the engine is `oilPrice >= tier.threshold`, so the threshold belongs to the tier above it: 49.990000 pays 14.9214 at 0.075000 while 50.000000 pays 19.8989 at 0.100000.

prompt: Why can a price multiplier sweep of the default project, run at 0.700000, 0.710000, 0.720000 and 0.800000, not settle which tier owns a threshold?
options: A sweep brackets a threshold and never lands on one: 0.710000 puts the price at 49.700000 and 0.720000 puts it at 50.400000, so no swept point is ever the threshold itself.
The sweep changes gross revenue at the same time as the rate, so the implied rate of royalty over gross revenue is contaminated and cannot be read.
The sweep reports the royalty only as a lifetime total, so no single year's rate can be recovered from it.
The multiplier is applied after the royalty is charged, so the tier a swept point selects belongs to the unswept deck price and not to the price printed.
explanation: The implied rate steps from 0.075000 to 0.100000 somewhere between the multipliers 0.710000 and 0.720000, and a bracket names an interval rather than a side.

prompt: A reader tries to place the default project's 70 USD per bbl deck exactly on a 50 USD per bbl threshold by choosing the multiplier 50 divided by 70. The sweep prints an applied price of 50.000000 and the implied rate reads 0.075000. What happened?
options: The engine rounds the applied price to six decimals before comparing it with the threshold, and a rounded 50.000000 is compared as a value strictly less than 50.
The applied price is 49.99999999999998 in binary floating point, strictly below the threshold, and six decimal places of printing hid the shortfall.
The multiplier is applied to the royalty rate rather than to the price, so the tier was selected from the unmultiplied 70 USD per bbl deck.
The threshold genuinely belongs to the tier below it, and the three probe decks at 49.990000, 50.000000 and 50.010000 are the exception rather than the rule.
explanation: Read a printed price column as a rounding of the price the engine used. The implied rate is the measurement, and 0.075000 says the engine was below 50.

prompt: `price_below_every_threshold` runs the default project at a 0.5 multiplier, putting oil at 35 USD per bbl against tiers of 60 USD/bbl at 12.5 percent and 80 USD/bbl at 15 percent. What royalty rate does the field pay?
options: Zero, because a tier list keyed at 60 and 80 USD per bbl charges nothing until the lower of the two keys is reached by the price.
The 15 percent rate of the upper tier, because with no threshold reached the walk falls through to the last entry in the list.
0.125000, but only from the year the deck's step hold lifts the applied price above the 60 USD/bbl key for the first time.
0.125000 in every year, which is the lowest tier's rate, charged as the fallback before any threshold is reached.
explanation: `getSlidingScaleRoyalty` falls back to the lowest tier's rate when the price has reached no threshold, which is why year 1 pays 18.0299 on gross revenue of 144.2389.

prompt: At a price multiplier of 1.200000 on the default project the PIA royalty charges 32.3089 on gross revenue of 323.0889. How much of that revenue was charged at 7.5 percent?
options: None of it. One tier is selected for the year and its rate is charged on the whole of gross revenue, with nothing left in the lower band.
The share of revenue attributable to the first 50 USD per bbl of price, with the remainder taken at 10 percent in the manner of an income tax bracket.
The gas and NGL portion of revenue, which stays in the first tier because only the oil price is allowed to select a tier above it.
The portion earned before the applied price crossed the threshold, which on a rising deck is the earlier years of the same run.
explanation: The implied rate at 1.200000 is 0.100000 on every dollar. A blended answer lands between the two printed royalties and looks reasonable, which is what makes it dangerous.

prompt: The teaching field ODIDI holds 45 USD per bbl through year 5 and steps to 65 at year 6. Under the PIA royalty its year 5 royalty is 5.7145 on gross revenue of 76.1939 and its year 6 royalty is 9.3986 on 93.9859. What moved?
options: Only the rate, since the oil volume is declining and the deck step merely holds gross revenue flat while the tier above takes over.
Only the revenue, because a deck that steps inside the life of a field cannot move a tier that was fixed when the regime was loaded.
Both the revenue and the rate: the deck lifted the price so revenue rose, and the same step carried the price past 50 so the implied rate went from 0.075000 to 0.100000.
The cost recovery limit released profit oil in that year, and the royalty follows the profit oil upward while the rate itself holds at 0.075000.
explanation: Two effects compound in one row. Revenue rises from 76.1939 to 93.9859 and the implied rate rises from 0.075000 to 0.100000, so the royalty rises by more than the price move alone.

prompt: `sliding_royalty_price_deck_crossing` runs a deck of 70 USD per bbl, 75 from year 5 and 80 from year 10 against tiers of 60 USD/bbl at 12.5 percent and 80 USD/bbl at 15 percent. Why does the rate not change in year 5?
options: Because the engine holds the tier chosen in year 1 for the whole of the life once cost recovery has begun against that year's revenue.
Because 75 USD per bbl has not reached the 80 USD/bbl threshold, so the deck's step moves the price without moving the tier.
Because a rate change is deferred to the year after the deck step, which is why the rate becomes 15 percent in year 10 rather than in year 9.
Because the deck's second point is a hold rather than a step, and `getPriceForYear` reads it as a continuation of the 70 USD per bbl point.
explanation: The rate holds at 12.5 percent until year 9 and becomes 15 percent from year 10. Two schedules run at once, one for price and one for rate, and they change in different years.

prompt: Under a sliding royalty, what selects the tier for a year?
options: The applied price of the highest-value stream in that year, so a gas-weighted field can be lifted into an upper tier by its Mscf price.
The boe-weighted average of the oil, gas and NGL prices, converted at 6000 scf per barrel before the thresholds are read.
Gross revenue for the year, which is why a larger field reaches an upper tier at a price a smaller field would not.
The applied oil price for that year, and nothing else.
explanation: Gas and NGL revenue is charged at whatever rate the oil price chose, and neither the gas price nor the NGL price can move it.

prompt: `price_below_every_threshold` pays 177.3774 million USD of royalty over its life on total revenue of 1419.0195, while contractor net cash flow reaches 80.8085 and NPV at 10 percent is negative 111.7254. What does that show about the instrument?
options: It shows the first tier's rate is charged only until the project's cumulative position turns negative, after which the royalty line stops.
It shows a royalty charged on gross revenue is refunded through the cost recovery pool whenever contractor net cash flow closes below the royalty total.
It has no relief mechanism: there is no minimum price below which the royalty is waived and no link at all to whether the field is making money.
It shows the instrument reduces its rate when cost recovery is failing, which is why the rate never rises above the first tier's 12.5 percent here.
explanation: A royalty larger than twice the contractor's whole lifetime cash flow was collected from a project that destroyed value, and 72.2941 million USD of cost was still unrecovered at the horizon.

prompt: A sweep prints an applied price column and an implied rate column. Which is the measurement of which side of a threshold the engine was on?
options: The applied price, because the tier is chosen from that price and the rate is only a consequence of the choice already made.
The implied rate, royalty over gross revenue, because it reports the tier the engine actually selected.
Neither, since both are derived columns rounded from full precision before printing.
The applied price, provided it is quoted to six decimals, which is enough places to separate any two thresholds a template uses.
explanation: A price printing as 50.000000 can be 49.99999999999998, and the implied rate of 0.075000 is what says so.

prompt: Across the default project sweep the PIA implied rate is 0.075000 at multipliers 0.500000, 0.600000, 0.700000 and 0.710000, and 0.100000 at 0.720000, 0.800000, 1.000000 and 1.200000. What is that pattern?
options: A step function with one break, flat inside each tier and discontinuous where the applied price crosses 50 USD per bbl.
A ramp that rises with price throughout, sampled coarsely enough at these eight multipliers that its slope looks flat inside each band.
A step that repeats at every multiple of the threshold, with a further break at 100 USD per bbl.
A progressive schedule whose average rate rises with price while the marginal rate holds.
explanation: Nothing between two thresholds is interpolated. The rate is 0.100000 at an applied price of 50.400000 and still 0.100000 at 84.000000.

prompt: The PIA template's lowest royalty tier is keyed at 0 USD/bbl. Why does that hide something a reader needs to check?
options: Because a threshold of 0 USD/bbl is skipped by the walk, leaving the 50 USD/bbl tier as the only rate the template can charge.
Because a zero threshold makes the implied rate undefined in any year the applied oil price is itself below one dollar.
Because the engine treats a 0 USD/bbl key as an instruction to charge no royalty until the next threshold in the list is reached.
Because at any positive price that tier is genuinely reached, so the fallback to the lowest tier's rate never shows itself and the selection looks like an ordinary threshold rule.
explanation: On tiers keyed at 60 and 80 USD/bbl the fallback is visible as 0.125000 charged below every threshold, and that is the entry every tier list has to be checked for.

prompt: What does `getSlidingScaleRoyalty` do with a tier list whose thresholds are not typed in ascending order?
options: It reads the list exactly as typed and keeps the last qualifying entry it meets, so a list written out of order charges the wrong rate for the year and raises nothing at all.
It sorts a copy before reading it, so the rate charged is the one keyed to the highest threshold the price has reached, whatever the typed order.
It rejects the regime outright, because a list whose thresholds do not ascend fails validation before any year is computed.
It reads the first and the last entry only, so a tier typed out of order in the middle of the list is passed over.
explanation: Selection is by threshold, from a sorted copy. The one table the engine does refuse is a list with two tiers at one threshold, and it names the repeated threshold rather than choosing between them.

prompt: A year's oil price has reached two of a royalty's thresholds. Which rate is charged?
options: The rate of whichever of the two qualifying tiers was typed last in the list.
The sum of the two rates, since every qualifying tier charges its own rate on gross revenue.
The rate keyed to the higher of the two thresholds, and the order the tiers were typed in makes no difference to it.
The rate of the lower of the two thresholds, since the selection stops at the first threshold the price has passed on its way up.
explanation: A sorted copy of the list is read, so the highest threshold reached is the one that governs. Nothing between two thresholds is interpolated and no rates are added.

prompt: The USA Gulf of Mexico template charges a flat 18.75 percent. What is its implied rate on the default project in year 25?
options: 0.187500, the same as in year 1, because a flat royalty carries a single rate and no price can move it.
Lower than 0.187500, because a flat rate is charged on gross revenue and gross revenue has declined through the life of the field.
Undefined, since the implied rate can only be computed in a year that carries capex in the same row.
0.187500 on oil revenue only, with the gas and NGL streams left outside the royalty base.
explanation: Year 1 charges 50.9979 million USD on gross revenue of 271.9889, and the ratio reads 0.187500 in year 1 and in year 25 alike.

prompt: On the Designer's default project year 1 gross revenue is 271.9889 million USD and royalty is 33.9986. A 100 percent cost recovery limit recovers 237.9903. What is the limit a percent of?
options: Gross revenue, which is why a 100 percent limit is described as recovering the whole of the year's revenue if the pool is deep enough.
Revenue after royalty, so a full limit takes everything left once the royalty has been removed.
The recoverable pool brought forward, so the limit caps the share of the outstanding balance that may be released in any one year.
Gross revenue less that year's opex, since opex is recovered first as an operating charge and only capex draws against the stated limit.
explanation: The royalty is taken first and never becomes recoverable cost, which is why the year 1 allowance at a full limit is 237.9903 and not 271.9889.

prompt: A published run caps cost recovery at 5 percent of revenue after royalty, so its cost pool never clears inside the 25 years. It records payback in year 3 all the same. How?
options: The engine treats the closing pool of 2543.7575 as a receivable and credits it to contractor cash in the year the horizon closes.
Payback is measured on gross revenue rather than on contractor net cash flow, so a project pays back whether or not any cost is recovered.
The 5 percent limit loosens automatically once the pool exceeds the capex, releasing the arrears in a single year and producing the year 3 payback.

Revenue the 5 percent limit will not release as cost oil becomes profit oil instead, and that regime gives the contractor the whole of the profit split, so the capital comes home through the profit share.
explanation: Cost recovery is not the only way a contractor is paid back. Total profit oil on that case is 5819.7423 against 3355.3781 on the full limit run, and contractor net cash flow still reaches 1530.0622 while its rate of return is null with the status multiple-roots.

prompt: On the Suite test project, `capped_5pct_pool_never_clears` pays total tax of 1745.9227 while `flat_test_project` pays 1006.6134. Why does the tighter cost recovery limit pay more tax?
options: Because cost recovered is not a tax deduction: the base is the contractor's profit share, and cost the limit refuses to release stays inside the profit oil the split and the tax act on.
Because an unrecovered pool is added to taxable income as a deemed benefit in the year the horizon closes, which raises the lifetime tax total.
Because the minimum tax provision binds whenever cost recovery falls short, and the minimum is charged on gross revenue rather than on the profit share.
Because the tighter limit lengthens the life of the pool, and the tax stack charges its capital uplift on every year a balance is still outstanding.
explanation: Recovering 306.3022 instead of 2770.6665 leaves 5819.7423 of profit oil rather than 3355.3781, and the tax follows the profit oil upward.

prompt: Cost recovered and profit oil are computed from the same base. What does a binding cost recovery limit change?
options: The total available to be shared, since revenue the limit refuses to release as cost oil is held back and paid out in no column of the ledger at all.
The royalty, because a lower limit leaves a larger residual on which the sliding scale charges its rate a second time.
Who receives the money and in which year, never how much of it there is, because cost recovered plus profit oil is always revenue after royalty.
The gross revenue of the year, since the engine reduces the applied price when the pool cannot be drawn down at the stated limit.
explanation: Profit oil is revenue after royalty minus cost recovered, floored at zero, so at a 100 percent limit on the default project year 1 profit oil is exactly 0.0000 and cost recovered is 237.9903.

prompt: The default project is run at cost recovery limits of 50, 80, 90 and 100 percent with nothing else changed. What are the lifetime totals?
options: Each limit recovers a different total, rising steadily from 940.4991 at 50 percent to 941.4436 at 100 percent as the allowance widens.
The 80, 90 and 100 percent runs are identical, each recovering 941.4436 and closing the pool at 0.0000, while the 50 percent run recovers 940.4991 and leaves 0.9444 unrecovered.
All four runs recover 941.4436, because the pool always clears inside the 25 year horizon whatever the annual allowance is.
The 50 and 80 percent runs are identical at 940.4991, and the 90 and 100 percent runs are identical at 941.4436.
explanation: Once the pool clears inside the life, the limit that cleared it faster changed when the money arrived and not how much of it arrived. Only the 50 percent run fails to finish.

prompt: At an 80 percent limit on the default project gross revenue falls from 271.9889 in year 1 to 171.8074 in year 6, while profit oil climbs from 47.5981 to 143.6310. What happened?
options: Production improved in the middle years, which lifts profit oil even as the price deck's step hold pulls gross revenue down.
The royalty rate fell as the applied price crossed back below a sliding threshold, leaving more revenue after royalty for the profit oil line.
The cost recovery limit tightens automatically once the contractor has passed payback, which diverts the allowance into profit oil.
The pool emptied. While the pool was deep the allowance ate the profit oil, and the moment there was nothing left to recover the profit oil was released.
explanation: Nothing improved and a balance simply ran out. The check is to read gross revenue beside profit oil: if revenue is falling while profit oil rises, the pool cleared.

prompt: At an 80 percent limit on the default project, cost recovered runs 190.3922, 171.1239, 153.8100, then 96.6215 in year 4 and 23.6264 in year 5. What is the year 5 figure?
options: That year's opex and nothing more, because the pool is empty and the only cost left to recover is the cost the year itself incurred.
The unrecovered balance carried out of year 4, released in full now that the allowance finally exceeds it.
Eighty percent of that year's revenue after royalty, which is the whole allowance the limit permits once the early capex has been worked off.
The straight line capital allowance the engine switches to once the pool has been drawn below the year's allowance.
explanation: Year 4 is the partial draw that empties the pool, and every year after it hands back that year's opex and passes the rest through as profit oil.

prompt: `capped_5pct_pool_never_clears` closes with 2543.7575 million USD still in the pool. What happens to it?
options: It is written off against the contractor's taxable profit share in year 25, which is why that case records a lower tax than the full limit run.
It is carried to a terminal settlement and added to contractor net cash flow in the final year, which is what makes payback possible in year 3.
Nothing. Nothing in the engine ever pays it, and the horizon does not extend to let the recovery finish.
It is converted into a loss carryforward that shelters the profit share in the years that follow, though the engine's 25 year horizon truncates it.
explanation: An unrecovered pool is not a receivable. A reader who adds it back values the case too highly by 2543.7575, and does the same to `capped_40pct` by 399.6419 and to `flat_test_project` by 79.3932.

prompt: `never_recovers_huge_capex` takes the Suite test project to 20000 of capex. Profit oil is 0.0000 in every year and total tax is 0.0000, yet government cash flow is 875.1492. Where did it come from?
options: It is the minimum tax, which is charged on gross revenue whenever the profit share falls to zero and no ordinary tax base exists.
All of it is royalty, which is charged on gross revenue and has nothing to do with whether any cost was recovered.
It is the government's share of the 6126.0445 of cost oil recovered.
It is a clawback of the earlier years' cost recovery, triggered when the closing pool of 15724.0151 exceeds the capex actually spent.
explanation: Total royalty on that case is 875.1492 and total tax is 0.0000, so the whole of government cash flow is the royalty. That is a royalty seen from the cost recovery side.

prompt: In year 5 the default project incurs 23.6264 of opex and no capex at all, yet at a 50 percent limit it recovers 83.6287. In year 1 it spends 500.0000 of capex and recovers 118.9951. What is the cost recovered column?
options: The year's own spend, capped at the allowance, which is why the year 1 figure is so much smaller than the capex that produced it.
The depreciation charge for the year, computed from the capex over a life the cost recovery limit implies.
The share of the year's spend the government has agreed to fund, with the balance left for the contractor to carry at its own risk.
A draw on a historic balance, so the year that recovers most may be a year that spent almost nothing.
explanation: A reader who treats cost recovered as a cost column will double count the whole of the year 1 capex of 500.0000 and then wonder why the totals refuse to close.

prompt: At a 50 percent cost recovery limit on the default project, cost recovered and profit oil are equal in every early row, 118.9951 and 118.9951 in year 1 and 106.9525 and 106.9525 in year 2. Why?
options: Because the engine splits revenue after royalty evenly between cost oil and profit oil in any year an unrecovered balance is still outstanding against the pool.
Because profit oil is defined as the mirror of cost recovered, which is an identity of cost recovery and holds at every limit.
Because the allowance is exactly half of revenue after royalty and the pool is deep enough to fill it, so the other half is what remains as profit oil.
Because the 50 percent limit is applied twice, once to the pool draw and once again to the profit oil that the draw leaves behind.
explanation: It is an arithmetic coincidence of a 50 percent limit and a deep pool, and any other limit breaks it: at 80 percent year 1 recovers 190.3922 and leaves 47.5981.

prompt: On the default project at limits of 80, 90 and 100 percent the total cost recovered over the life is 941.4436 million USD. What is that number made of?
options: The life's capex of 500.0000 and its opex of 441.4436, taken together, because every dollar comes back and the limit only decides when.
The capex of 500.0000 plus the share of opex the allowance was able to release before the pool cleared in year 3 or year 4.
The undepreciated balance of the capex, since opex is expensed against profit oil rather than entering the recoverable pool at all.
The lifetime allowance, which is the stated percent of the whole life's revenue after royalty and is therefore a different total at each of the four limits.
explanation: There is no capital allowance, no life, no method and no schedule. Capex enters the pool whole in the year it is spent and leaves when revenue after royalty makes room.

prompt: What does the cost recovery limit cap?
options: The pool, so a balance can never grow beyond the stated percent of the life's revenue after royalty.
The annual draw, and nothing else.
The total ever recovered, which is why a tight limit leaves a permanent shortfall against the capex spent.
The share of the year's revenue after royalty available to the contractor once its profit split has also been applied.
explanation: It does not vary with the R factor, the price or the year, and a regime that recovers capex and opex at different limits cannot be expressed at all.

prompt: Undiscounted contractor net cash flow on the default project is 986.7327 at a 100 percent limit and 986.4494 at a 50 percent limit. What should a reader conclude about a tighter limit?
options: That it makes no difference at all, since an undiscounted total is the only honest measure of what a regime is worth to a contractor.
That it costs the contractor money in proportion to the tightening, which the undiscounted totals understate because they are nominal.
That it costs the contractor time rather than money, right up to the point where the pool fails to clear inside the horizon.
That the two figures differ only by the engine's own arithmetic noise.

prompt: Which band does `calculateIRR` search, and what does it hand back when that band holds no single root?
options: Negative 99 to 1000 percent, and null with a status word naming the reason.
Zero to 1000 percent, and the top of the band, so the largest rate it can represent stands in for the root it could not find.
Negative 99 to 1000 percent, and 0.0000 percent, which is the value the function has always used where a search comes up empty.
One hundred percent doubled ten times, and the top of that bracket whenever the present value is still positive there.
explanation: A number comes back only when exactly one rate in the band brings the present value to zero. The four words that come back instead are no-sign-change, no-root, above-clamp and multiple-roots.

prompt: The published case with flows of negative 1 then 2000 has a root at 199900.0000 percent. What does the engine report for it?
options: 199900.0000 percent, since the root is exact and the band is a search hint rather than a limit on what may be reported.
Null, with the status above-clamp, because the only root sits beyond the top of the band the engine searches.
1000.0000 percent, the top of the band, which is the nearest rate the engine is prepared to defend.
The top of a doubling search that started at 100 percent, since a bracket that stopped short is still the engine's fallback.
explanation: `irr_above_clamp_inside_old_bracket`, with flows of negative 100 then 1500, has a root of 1400.0000 percent and the same status, so a root the retired bisection would have printed is refused as well.

prompt: What tells a reader that the engine refused to name a rate rather than failing to find one?
options: A rate of 0.0000 percent, which is the value the function returns whenever its search comes up empty.
A suspiciously round rate where a rate should be, which is the edge of a search printed as though it were an answer.
The absence of any entry at all, since a refusal leaves the field out of the result object rather than writing to it.
The status word printed beside the null, which names which of the four reasons for declining applies here.
explanation: A null is a decision and not a gap. `irrRoots` carries the roots inside the band when there are several of them, and `irrRootAboveBand` flags one beyond it.

prompt: Two published cases used to report 0.0000 percent, one worth 25.6198 million USD at 10 percent and one worth negative 16.5289. What do they report now?
options: 0.0000 percent for both, since the repair changed the statuses the engine records and not the rates it prints.
Null with the status no-sign-change for the first, and the negative root itself, negative 10.0000 percent, for the second.
Null with the status no-root for both, since neither of them has a rate the engine is willing to name.
Null with the status above-clamp for the first and null with the status multiple-roots for the second.
explanation: One project never loses and the other never wins, and the retired rule printed the same four characters for both.

prompt: A reader sees an empty rate column on several regimes of one comparison and reads it as a set of projects that broke even. What is wrong with that reading?
options: Nothing, provided the present value at a rate of zero is checked as well, because the same statuses fire on a project sitting at break even.
Only the precision, since the column would print four decimals on a rate the engine had actually found.
A null is the engine declining to name a rate, and none of its reasons for declining has anything to do with breaking even.
It confuses the rate with the payout year, which is the first year the R factor rises above 1.0.
explanation: All six templates on the teaching field come back null, and their present values at 12 percent run from negative 5.8662 to negative 58.1813 million USD.

prompt: What goes wrong when a comparison is sorted or filtered on the internal rate of return column?
options: Every regime whose rate is null is left unranked, and a filter set above a threshold drops the hopeless projects and the ones that needed no capital together.
The sort puts the largest rate at the top, which on this engine is always the edge of a search rather than a root, so the order the comparison ends up in is upside down.
The sort disagrees with a sort on present value, which is the ranking the summary is built on.
Nothing, so long as the negative rates are read as the losses they stand for before the column is sorted.
explanation: The case with capex of 20000 comes back null with the status no-root, on a contractor net cash flow of negative 15724.0151 million USD and a present value of negative 15453.8510.

prompt: The capex multiplier of 0.7 on the flat regime has a present value of zero at 1095.4783 percent and again at negative 20.4852 percent. What does the engine report?
options: 1095.4783 percent, since the reduced outlay came back almost immediately and the rate is a genuine root of those flows.
Null with the status multiple-roots, with `irrRoots` listing the negative root alone and `irrRootAboveBand` flagging the other.
Negative 20.4852 percent, the only root inside the band, since a root beyond the band is outside the engine's business.
The 1000 percent clamp the screening engine next door applies, which is what the top edge of the band returns.
explanation: One root inside the band and one above it is still more than one root, so no single rate is named. The case pays back a reduced outlay in year 2 and reaches its payout year in year 1.

prompt: Which statement about what the internal rate of return function hands back is correct?
options: It returns one number and no status, so a guard, a bound and a genuine root arrive at the call site indistinguishable from one another.
It returns the edge of the band whenever a root lies beyond it, so a reported 1000.0000 percent is how the engine says above-clamp.
It returns either one rate or a null with a status, and where several roots are in reach it lists the ones inside the band.
It returns 0.0000 percent for a project whose only root is negative, since the column carries no negative rates at all.
explanation: A negative root inside the band is reported as the negative rate it is, and negative 10.0000 percent on the published case of negative 100 then 90 is the example.

prompt: A comparison of several regimes on one field is put in front of you. What is written down before any number is read?
options: The headline reading of each regime, which is its present value at the field's own rate beside its rate of return and its payback year.
The four instruments of each regime: its royalty, its cost recovery limit, its profit split and its tax stack.
The field's own production profile and price deck, which every regime in the comparison shares.
The order the summary has sorted the regimes into, because that order is the engine's own verdict on the comparison.
explanation: Two lines of instruments predict most of what the ledgers will do. On the teaching field a flat 0 percent royalty, a 50 percent limit and a tiered split already say what kind of ledger Angola - Deepwater PSC will return.

prompt: Angola - Deepwater PSC carries a flat 0 percent royalty, a 50 percent recovery limit, an R factor split of 70, 50 and 30 percent and a stack of 25 and 50 percent. Which of those leaves 192.1146 million USD in the pool at the close of the teaching field?
options: The flat 0 percent royalty, since a regime that takes nothing off gross revenue has no mechanism for returning capital either.
The resource rent tax at 50 percent, whose relief is drawn against the cost recovery pool and holds that balance open.
The R factor split, which hands the contractor a smaller share of profit oil as the ratio climbs and so slows the return of capital.
The 50 percent recovery limit.
explanation: Angola recovers 618.0991 million USD on that field against 790.8868 for Brazil - Concession, whose limit is 100 percent. The limit decides how fast the pool can drain and nothing else in the list does.

prompt: Under one template the implied royalty rate on the teaching field reads 0.187500 in year 1 and 0.187500 in year 25. Under another it reads 0.075000 in years 1 to 5 and 0.100000 from year 6. Which reading identifies the instrument?
options: The one that changes inside the life, because a rate that moves mid field is a sliding scale and the year it moves is a price event.
The one that holds, because only a flat royalty can charge the same rate in year 1 and in year 25 of a declining field.
Neither, because an implied rate is royalty over gross revenue and that ratio is fixed by the price deck rather than by the tier list.
The one that changes, because a royalty rate that moves inside a life is following the production decline through the variable opex.
explanation: A sliding royalty sitting below every threshold reads as constant as a flat one, so a rate that holds proves nothing. Year 1 pays 26.1856 million USD on 139.6563 and year 25 pays 1.2953 on 6.9081 under the flat 18.75 percent.

prompt: Ghana - Deepwater recovers 788.5887 million USD on the teaching field and closes with 21.6250 still in the pool. Which of those two figures is read first?
options: The recovery total, since it is the number the ledger reports and the pool is derived from it by subtraction.
Neither on its own. The two have to be added, because the sum of them is the cost the contractor actually incurred over the life.
The closing pool, because a recovery total says nothing until you know how much was never paid back.
The recovery total, because the closing pool is settled against government cash flow at the horizon.
explanation: Angola - Deepwater PSC recovers 618.0991 and closes at 192.1146 on the same field. A large closing pool is money the contractor spent that the ledger never paid back.

prompt: The Professional tier ends on one sentence about instruments. What does it say?
options: An instrument is only as good as the ledger it is read on, so a regime has to be compared on more than one field before it is ranked.
An instrument's rate never tells you what it collects. Its base does.
An instrument's rate ranks its burden whenever two regimes are run on the same project with the same production and the same price deck.
An instrument that cannot be expressed in the four fields should be approximated by raising the rate of one that can.
explanation: A corporate income tax of 21 percent collected 260.7539 million USD on the default project where one of 35 percent collected 230.9340, because the two rates were charged on different bases.

prompt: Every one of the six templates returns a negative present value on the teaching field at 12 percent. How is that reported?
options: As one fact about the field, that its cash flows carry no 12 percent return under any of the six regimes, rather than as six separate failures.
As six loss making regimes, since a negative present value on a 25 year ledger is the model's report of a loss.
As evidence that the field's own discount rate has been set too high, because a rate that no regime in the comparison can beat is not a screening rate at all.
As an artefact of year end discounting, which is the more conservative of the two conventions in the package.
explanation: Brazil - Concession is the least negative at negative 5.8662 million USD, and it returns 192.9896 undiscounted with payback in year 6. No regime on that field carries a single rate of return at all.

prompt: The summary of a comparison is sorted by contractor net present value descending. What can be read off a regime's position in it?
options: That the last row is the heaviest regime for the contractor, since government cash flow runs in the reverse order of contractor present value.
That the rows are in order of rate of return as well, because the two measures rank the same cash flows on the same ledger.
That the rows are in order of payback, since a regime that returns capital faster carries more of its cash in the early discounted years.
That the first row is the best regime for the contractor, and nothing else.
explanation: On the teaching field the sort puts Brazil - Concession first and Angola - Deepwater PSC last, while government cash flow runs the other way at 316.7898 million USD for Angola against 232.9950 for Brazil.

prompt: A reading is handed over as the figure 192.9896 million USD, and another as negative 5.8662. What is missing from each?
options: The units, since millions of USD and percent cannot sit beside each other.
The sign convention, because a contractor cash flow and a present value are reported with opposite signs by this engine.
The regime on the first and the discount rate on the second, and without them neither figure is an answer.
The year, since both are lifetime totals over a fixed horizon.
explanation: Both belong to Brazil - Concession on the teaching field, the first as undiscounted contractor net cash flow over the life and the second as its present value at 12 percent.

prompt: The seven step reading has been worked end to end on a field and every number is labelled. What does the method still refuse to produce?
options: A recommendation. It says what each regime does to this ledger and never which one a government should offer or a contractor should sign.
A comparison across regimes, since each ledger is worked on its own and the steps do not put two of them side by side.
A present value, because the method stops at the undiscounted totals and leaves the discounting to a separate reading.
A reading of the tax stack, since the four fields cannot express what a real fiscal code charges.
explanation: The sandbox is not a second fiscal truth. It compares the shape of regimes against each other, and a number lifted out of it and quoted as a liability is worth nothing.

prompt: The comparison summary carries government share of net revenue, and Brazil - Concession reads 27.5413 percent on the teaching field. What should a reader know about that column before quoting it?
options: It is government cash flow divided by gross revenue, so it is not comparable with a headline tax rate at all.
Government take, the same government cash flow divided without the capex added back, sits in the same result object and appears on the screen too.
It is the rate the tax column implies, so it can be checked by dividing total tax by total profit oil on the same ledger.
It is reported only for regimes whose profit oil is positive in every year, so a comparison of six can carry fewer than six values.
explanation: Two ratios of one government cash flow live in one result and both are on the screen. Working out which is which is where the next tier starts, and the six on that field run from 27.5413 to 37.4463 percent.

prompt: The capex sweep on the teaching field runs eight multipliers from 0.8 to 1.5, the last of them exactly 1.5. What does the resilience verdict built on it price?
options: Every overrun the project could suffer, since the sweep is run to the point where the least resilient regime stops paying back.
The overrun at which the best regime for the contractor changes.
The contractor present value given up between a 20 percent underspend and a 50 percent overrun, which is the range the axis claims.
A cost overrun measured against the closing pool, because an overrun that cannot be recovered is the only kind that reaches the contractor.
explanation: Over those eight points Ghana - Deepwater gives up 181.1922 million USD of contractor present value and Angola - Deepwater PSC 252.6075. Until the 2026-09-15 repair the loop stopped at 1.4 and every resilience figure was understated.

prompt: Across the swept prices on the teaching field government take climbs 1.9971 points for Ghana - Deepwater and falls 37.6994 for USA - Gulf of Mexico. What does a falling share mean?
options: That the government collects less money as price rises.
That the regime is charging a sliding royalty in reverse, since only a rate that falls with price can produce a falling share.
That the sweep has run below the range where the regime's instruments bind, so the share is falling towards the level it holds at low price.
That the regime hands the upside to the contractor as price rises.
explanation: A share is a ratio and not an amount. The regime whose share climbs fastest is the progressive one, and on that field it is Brazil - Concession at 7.4752 points.

prompt: The verdict named best for the contractor on the teaching field is Brazil - Concession, whose present value there is negative 5.8662 million USD. What is that verdict saying?
options: That Brazil is the least bad of the six, which is a real answer to a real question and not the question most readers think they asked.
That Brazil returns a positive present value once the negative sign is read as a convention of the summary column.
That the verdict is unusable, since a ranking of six negative numbers cannot name a best regime at all.
That the field is uneconomic under every regime, so the verdict is about the field rather than about Brazil.
explanation: Every rate of return on that field is below the 12 percent it is discounted at. Being least bad is worth saying out loud, with its label attached.

prompt: Three habits from the Professional tier carry into a six regime comparison. What are they?
options: Sort on present value, then on rate of return, then on payback, so that a verdict is never made on one column alone.
Name the base before the rate, read the closing pool before believing a cost recovery total, and write down what a zero means before quoting it.
Convert every regime to a common government take, discount at one rate, and report the range rather than a point.
Check the price deck, the production profile and the cost columns, since a comparison is only as good as the inputs the regimes share.
explanation: Each habit answers a way this package has already misled a reader: a 21 percent rate that collected more than a 35 percent one, a recovery total with 2543.7575 million USD left unpaid behind it, and a rate column that once printed 0.0000 percent for two opposite things.

prompt: On the teaching field under the PIA template the pool clears in year 9 and stands at 0.0000 through year 18, then reads 0.5221 million USD in year 19 and 30.5883 at the close of year 25. What reopened it?
options: A second round of capex late in the life, which enters the pool whole in the year it is spent as the first round did.
The royalty rate stepping up in year 19, which reduced revenue after royalty below the level the limit needs to clear a year's cost.
Revenue fell far enough that the allowance no longer covered the year's own cost, so the shortfall began accruing again.
The uplift on the resource rent tax, which adds whatever relief it has not used to the cost pool in the years the tax is zero.
explanation: In year 19 the allowance releases 12.3236 million USD against a cost of 12.8457, and the difference of that year and every year after it is what carries the pool to 30.5883.
